onesie is a command line tool that asks System One models typed questions about text. It needs the
`onesie` binary on PATH and an API key, from TypeSafe, OpenRouter, Berget, Levanto, Cloudflare or
Vercel. This skill walks a user from nothing to a working first command.

There are two ways in. A user who installs onesie first can add the plugin afterwards. A user who
installs the plugin first gets a session start line saying onesie is missing or has no key, and this
skill takes it from there.

The steps, in order:

1. Check what is there already: `command -v onesie`, then `onesie profile show`.
2. Install onesie if it is missing, per the install section below.
3. Ask which provider the user has an account with.
4. Have the user store the key in a profile, outside the conversation.
5. Run `onesie profile test` and confirm it reports the provider and a model count.

For a flag this skill does not cover, run `onesie help all`, `onesie profile --help` or
`onesie help calibrate all`, and `onesie version` for the version and the built in limits.

## Rules

### Never ask for the key in chat. The user stores it with onesie profile create, outside the conversation.

Anything typed into the conversation is sent to the model and kept in the transcript. `onesie profile create NAME --provider PROVIDER` reads the key from a hidden prompt in a real terminal, or from stdin otherwise, and never prints it. So ask the user to run it in their own terminal, or to pipe the key from a password manager, as in `pass show typesafe | head -n 1 | onesie profile create work --provider typesafe`. `pass show` and its siblings print metadata after the secret, and `profile create` refuses stdin that holds more than one non blank line, so keep the `head -n 1`. A command that reads from a password manager is safe to run for them, since only stderr lines naming the keychain item or the file come back.

### Ask which account the user has, TypeSafe, OpenRouter, Berget, Levanto, Cloudflare or Vercel, before storing a key.

A profile names its provider, so `onesie profile create work --provider openrouter` makes an OpenRouter profile. The first profile becomes the default, and a run with no `--profile` uses the default. An exported key variable, `ONESIE_BASE_URL` or `TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL` beats the default profile, with a notice on stderr, so set `ONESIE_PROFILE=NAME` to keep the profile ahead of them. On a custom base URL, a profile's key never goes to one from a variable, the default profile's key never goes to a typed `--base-url`, and a key variable never goes to a profile's `base_url`. To switch to another profile, run `onesie profile use NAME`. Do not export `ONESIE_PROVIDER` for a stored key, since `--provider` and `ONESIE_PROVIDER` run without a profile and read only the provider's key variable. For cloudflare, pass the account too, as in `onesie profile create cf --provider cloudflare --account-id ACCOUNT_ID`. `--model` stores the model a run uses when it names none.

### End the setup with onesie profile test, not profile show.

`profile show` only reports what a run would use and where its key lives, and never reads the keychain. `profile test` reads the key and sends it to the provider's model listing, which costs no tokens, then prints `profile:`, `provider:`, `key:` and `models:` with a count. On berget it also asks one tiny question with the profile's model, which spends a few tokens. It exits 2 when no key resolves on the provider's own base URL, 3 when the provider refuses the key or the keychain cannot give it up, and 4 or 5 when the provider cannot be reached. Only a clean `profile test` means the next real command will work.

### For a server of the user's own, set ONESIE_BASE_URL and store no key.

A base URL other than the provider's own needs no key, and a run with none sends no `Authorization` header. So for a model served on this machine, such as ollaya on `http://localhost:11435`, `ONESIE_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11435` points every run at it with nothing to store. A profile can hold the same setup: `onesie profile create local --provider typesafe --base-url http://localhost:11435` with the key prompt left empty prints that the profile holds no key. A server that wants a key answers 401, which exits 3 and says no key was sent. `onesie profile show` names where the base URL came from.

## Installing onesie

Three ways work. Prefer Homebrew when the user has it.

- The Homebrew formula, `brew install frodi-karlsson/tap/onesie`.
- The install script,
  `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/frodi-karlsson/onesie/main/install.sh | sh`. It
  checks the sha256 of the download, installs to `~/.local/bin` or to `$ONESIE_INSTALL_DIR`, and
  warns when that directory is not on PATH.
- A Go toolchain, at the version `go.mod` names or newer, with
  `go install github.com/frodi-karlsson/onesie/cmd/onesie@latest`. It writes the binary to `$GOBIN`,
  or to `$(go env GOPATH)/bin` when that is unset, which is often not on PATH. If
  `command -v onesie` still finds nothing, have the user add that directory to PATH in their shell
  profile and open a new shell.

Prefer these three to a download from the releases page, which leaves the user to unpack the archive
and put the binary on PATH by hand.

Confirm the install with `onesie version`, which prints the version, the commit, the build date and the
built in limits.

## Storing the key

| provider | command | env var alternative |
| --- | --- | --- |
| typesafe | `onesie profile create work --provider typesafe` | `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` |
| openrouter | `onesie profile create work --provider openrouter` | `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` |
| berget | `onesie profile create work --provider berget` | `BERGET_API_KEY` |
| levanto | `onesie profile create work --provider levanto` | `LEVANTO_API_KEY` |
| cloudflare | `onesie profile create work --provider cloudflare --account-id ACCOUNT_ID` | `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN`, with `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` |
| vercel | `onesie profile create work --provider vercel` | `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` |

A name in place of `work` is 1 to 64 lowercase letters, digits, `-` or `_`, does not start with `-`,
and is not `none`. A profile holds the provider, its key, and optionally `--model`, the model a run
uses when it names none, and `--base-url`, or `--account-id` on cloudflare. The first profile
becomes the default, and `onesie profile use NAME` changes it. [Choosing a profile][choosing] gives
the order a run picks a profile in. `--provider` or `ONESIE_PROVIDER` runs without a profile and
reads only the provider's env var, which suits CI.

A server of the user's own needs no key. With `ONESIE_BASE_URL`, `--base-url` or a profile's
`base_url` set to anything but the provider's own, a run with no key sends none, and an empty key at
the `profile create` prompt stores a profile that holds no key.

Profiles live in `profiles.json`, in the config dir [profiles.json][file] names. The file is written
at mode 600, and a directory it creates at mode 700. When there is an OS keychain the key goes
there, under the service `onesie`, and the profile only names the item. `--file` keeps the key in
the file itself. A `credentials.json` there is converted into profiles the first time onesie
reads it. `onesie profile list` lists the profiles, `onesie profile update NAME --key` stores a new
key, and `onesie profile delete NAME` removes a profile and its keychain item. `profile update`
changes any member in place, so a profile never needs deleting to fix it. `--provider` keeps the
base URL, account id and model, and needs `--key` on a profile that holds a key. `--name NEW` renames it. An
empty key typed at the `--key` prompt drops the key from a profile whose base URL is not the
provider's own, and an empty key piped on stdin never drops one.

[choosing]: https://github.com/frodi-karlsson/onesie/blob/main/REFERENCE.md#choosing-a-profile
[file]: https://github.com/frodi-karlsson/onesie/blob/main/REFERENCE.md#profilesjson

`profile create` writes only to stderr, never the key:

| stderr line | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `stored the key in the OS keychain as NAME@...` | the key is in the keychain, and the profile names the item |
| `NAME is the default profile, since it is the first` | the first profile became the default |
| `onesie: warning: ... The key is in PATH instead` | the keychain refused, so the key went into the file |
| `the keychain did not answer in time` | a keychain prompt waited over 10 seconds, and the file was not written. Have the user answer the prompt and run the command again, or pass `--file` |
| `stdin carries more than one line` | the piped input held more than the key. Pipe it through `head -n 1` |
| `is readable or writable by its group or others` | the existing `profiles.json` is readable or writable by its group or others. Have the user run `chmod 600` on it |
| `converted credentials.json into profiles.json` | an older key file became profiles, named after their providers |

## Installing the plugin

In Claude Code:

```
/plugin marketplace add frodi-karlsson/onesie
/plugin install onesie@onesie
```

The plugin adds the onesie skills and a session start line that reports whether onesie is on PATH,
whether a key resolves, whether `onesie version` differs from the release the skills describe, and
which question files `-f` finds. It never blocks a command.
